newsitem.title: south korea: S.Korean bribery trial drags in presidential aides.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean bribery trial drags in presidential aides.

text.p: A South Korean court on Monday heard testimony that top aides to President Kim Young-sam discussed improper bank loans worth hundreds of millions of dollars to bankrupt Hanbo Steel Co.

The testimony came on the opening day of a bribery trial involving 10 people, including Hanbo Group founder Chung Tae-soo, a former cabinet minister, ruling and opposition party lawmakers and top bankers.
South Korea's number two steelmaker crumbled in January under debts of $5.8 billion in the country's biggest corporate failure. Prosecutors allege Chung offered kickbacks to keep loans rolling in.
The scandal rocked the nation, stained Kim's reputation for fighting graft and forced him into a sweeping reshuffle of his cabinet and New Korea Party leadership.
In a separate development, Kim's son who is being hounded by the opposition over his role in the Hanbo affair, issued an apology and said he was willing to accept punishment.
Kim Hyun-chul, in begging forgiveness, made no direct reference to the loans scandal or a separate furore involving allegations he meddled in administration appointments.
His father apologised for the Hanbo crisis on television last month and said he felt shame that his second son had been dragged into the scandal.
One of the defendants in Monday's trial, ruling party lawmaker Hong In-gil, admitted pocketing 1 billion won ($1.14 million) in payments from Chung to arrange loans to keep Hanbo Steel afloat.
He was asked several times by prosecutors whether he solicited help from economic secretaries in the presidential Blue House for loans. Each time he answered yes.

After each question, Hong was asked whether he was aware that money subsequently flowed to Hanbo from banks. Again, he answered yes. The total amount of loans involved was 690 billion won ($784 million).
One of the aides, Han Yi-horn, served in 1994. The other, Lee Suk-chae, was dismissed last month.
Former home affairs minister Kim Woo-suk acknowledged he took up to 200 million won from Chung, but insisted it was not a bribe.
The cash was stashed in crates covered with apples and placed in the trunk of his car while the two were at dinner, Kim told the court.

Three bankers on trial acknowledged they also received money in apple crates from Chung, who faces charges of embezzling 213.6 billion won, fraud, issuing bad cheques and violating laws on trust and savings companies.
Opposition parties allege the president's son, who holds no official post, used his position to help win loans for Hanbo.
"Lowering my head, I deeply apologise to the people and solicit forgiveness," Kim Hyun-chul said in a statement.
"I also apologise to my father for my failure to fulfil my filial duty as a son."

"I wanted to help my father but as a consequence made the mistake of causing trouble to father and anxiety to the people. I am deeply repentant now," the statement said. He said he "wept profusely" during his father's apology.
State prosecutors exonerated Kim Hyun-chul in a probe into Hanbo's collapse, but the opposition slammed the investigation as a whitewash and demanded a new inquiry.
Kim Hyun-chul said he was prepared to testify before parliament and would agree to a new prosecution probe into his role in the Hanbo affair.
"I will willingly accept any punishment if I was in the wrong," he said. (Conversion: $1 = 880 won)
